Kronecker Products, Polarity Quotients and Large Graph Constructions

Kelly Isham Address: Colgate University, Hamilton, NY Email address: kisham@colgate.edu , Kartik Lakhotia Address: Intel, Santa Clara, CA Email address: kartik.lakhotia@intel.com , Laura Monroe Address: Los Alamos National Laboratory, Los Alamos, NM Email address: lmonroe@lanl.gov and Fabrizio Petrini Address: Intel, Santa Clara, CA Email address: fabrizio.petrini@intel.com
Abstract.

In this paper, we establish a structural compatibility between the Kronecker product of bipartite graphs that admit polarity and their polarity quotients, and provide a sharp upper bound on the diameter of these graphs. We use these properties to construct new families of graphs, all of which have orders that asymptotically approach the Moore bound.

We show that the bipartite compatibility graphs have a natural polarity, and that the corresponding polarity quotients comprise a new family of graphs of any even diameter 2​k2k with degree (q+1)k(q+1)^{k} for any prime power qq, much smaller than those of other known families of that diameter and field order qq. These families generalize the Erdős-Rényi-Brown polarity graphs. Kronecker products of these polarity quotients give another new family of graphs of any even diameter for every pair of prime powers q,rq,r.

Certain generalized polygons are known to admit polarity with polarity quotients approaching the Moore bound asymptotically. Kronecker products of these polarity quotients give another new family of graphs of diameters 22, 33 and 55, including a diameter-33 degree-1818 graph of order larger than any previously known for that degree and diameter.

1. Introduction

1.1. Motivation and Results

In this paper, we address the problem of finding large graphs of a given degree and diameter, known as the degree-diameter problem, with especial emphasis on graphs that approach the Moore bound, the mathematical upper bound on graph order for a given degree and diameter.

We have constructed two different new families of graphs whose orders approach the Moore bound for every even diameter, one of which generalizes the well-known diameter-22 Erdős-Rényi-Brown polarity graphs [21, 12] to graphs of any even diameter by taking polarity quotients of bipartite compatibility graphs. This family has degrees asymptotically as small as the fourth root of those in the related halved-flag graphs discussed in [14] at the same diameter and field order.

The second family uses Kronecker products of the polarity quotients of the bipartite compatibility graphs and in so doing, broadens the range of possible degrees for any even diameter. We have also constructed new families of graphs using a similar Kronecker construction of diameters {2,3,5}\{2,3,5\} based on generalized polygons.

We accomplish the Kronecker construction in part through structural theorems showing compatibility between the Kronecker product on bipartite graphs and their polarity quotients, and then establishing exact diameters for certain graphs and a multiplicative rule for the asymptotic fractions of the Moore bound.

1.2. Three New Large Constructions

We show three new constructions in this section that approach the Moore bound, two based on the bipartite compatibility graphs of [14] and the other based on generalized polygons.

1.2.1. Polarity Quotients of Bipartite Compatibility Graphs (Diameter 2​k2k)

We show that the bipartite compatibility graphs ℂ⁡(k,q)\mathbb{C}(k,q) [14] admit a natural polarity, and that their polarity quotients approach the Moore bound asymptotically for every even diameter 2​k2k. These graphs have the added advantage that their degrees are much smaller than the degrees of the even-diameter graphs in [14]: for the same diameter 2​k2k and field order qq, they have exact degree (q+1)k(q+1)^{k}, asymptotically the 4t​h4^{th} root of the degrees of the even-diameter H2​k,qH_{2k,q} graphs from [14], which are asymptotic to (q+1)4​k(q+1)^{4k}. We thus derive the following theorem:

Theorem 1.1.

Let qq be a prime power and let k∈ℤ>1.k\in\mathbb{Z}_{>1}. Then the bipartite compatibility graph ℂ⁡(k,q)\mathbb{C}(k,q) admits a polarity β\beta, and its polarity quotient graph Pβ​(ℂ​(k,q))¯\overline{P_{\beta}(\mathbb{C}(k,q))} has diameter 2​k2k and degree (q+1)k.(q+1)^{k}. The orders of the graphs Pβ​(ℂ​(k,q))¯\overline{P_{\beta}(\mathbb{C}(k,q))} are [2​k+1]q!(q+1)k\frac{[2k+1]_{q}!}{(q+1)^{k}} and approach the Moore bound as q→∞.q\rightarrow\infty.

These graphs are discussed in Section 6.

1.2.2. Kronecker Products of Polarity Quotients of Bipartite Compatibility Graphs (Diameter 2​k2k)

The diameter results on the polarity quotients of the bipartite compatibility graphs allow us to use the theoretical results in Section 5 to construct Kronecker-product graphs that approach the Moore bound asymptotically for every even diameter 2​k2k, by using polarity quotients of the bipartite compatibility graphs as factors. These products have degree (q+1)k​(r+1)k(q+1)^{k}(r+1)^{k}, where qq and rr are prime powers, and have degree (q+1)2​k(q+1)^{2k} when q=rq=r, asymptotically the square root of the degrees of the H2​k,qH_{2k,q} graphs from [14]. Also, since these allow any pair q,rq,r of prime powers, the set of admissible degrees is larger than that in [14]. This is discussed in Section 6.

Theorem 1.2.

Let qq and rr be prime powers and let k∈ℤ>1.k\in\mathbb{Z}_{>1}. Then the polarity quotients of Reduced-Kronecker products of bipartite compatibility graphs Pβ​(ℂ⁡(k,q)⊙ℂ⁡(k,r))¯\overline{P_{\beta}(\mathbb{C}(k,q)\odot\mathbb{C}(k,r))} form an infinite family of graphs each having diameter 2​k2k and degree (q+1)k​(r+1)k.(q+1)^{k}(r+1)^{k}. The orders of the graphs Pβ​(ℂ⁡(k,q)⊙ℂ⁡(k,r))¯\overline{P_{\beta}(\mathbb{C}(k,q)\odot\mathbb{C}(k,r))} are [2​k+1]q!⋅[2​k+1]r!(q+1)k​(r+1)k\frac{[2k+1]_{q}!\cdot[2k+1]_{r}!}{(q+1)^{k}(r+1)^{k}} and approach the Moore bound as q,r→∞.q,r\rightarrow\infty.

1.2.3. Kronecker Products of Polarity Quotients of Generalized Polygons (Diameters 2,3,52,3,5)

Generalized polygons 𝔾n​(q,q)\mathbb{G}_{n}(q,q) are known to admit polarity when n∈{2,3,4,6}n\in\{2,3,4,6\} and qq is an integer satisfying certain conditions that depend on nn. Polarity quotients of non-digon generalized polygons also satisfy the theorems and corollaries in Section 5, so may be used as factors in Kronecker products for another set of graph families that approach the Moore bound asymptotically for diameters in {2,3,5}.\{2,3,5\}. We discuss this in Section 7, and address other types of generalized polygons not always treated in the existing literature, such as digons and thin generalized polygons. Using this construction we get a degree-1818 diameter-33 graph that is the largest known at time of writing, with 23402340 vertices.

1.3. Kronecker Products and Polarity Quotients: Structure, Diameter and Order

Here and throughout the paper, the Kronecker, or direct, product of graphs HH and KK has vertex set H×KH\times K and edges ((h1,k1),(h2,k2))((h_{1},k_{1}),(h_{2},k_{2})) if and only if (h1,h2)∈EH(h_{1},h_{2})\in E_{H} and (k1,k2)∈EK(k_{1},k_{2})\in E_{K}. This product is denoted H⊗KH\otimes K. We assume that the factor graphs HH and KK are undirected and connected with no multiedges, but we allow loops. A polarity on a bipartite graph 𝔾⁡(U=(A,B),𝔼)\mathbb{G}(U=(A,B),\mathbb{E}) is an involutional automorphism ρ\rho that reverses the partition. ℍ⊙𝕂\mathbb{H}\odot\mathbb{K} denotes one of the two isomorphic components of ℍ⊗𝕂\mathbb{H}\otimes\mathbb{K} (as defined in Section 4.3). Finally, when we use the term degree of a graph, we mean the maximum degree of all the vertices.

1.3.1. Structural Result

We begin with the isomorphism that is the basis for the theoretical results in this paper. Theorem 1.3 is closely related to earlier factorization results for bipartite graphs with bipartition-reversing involutions from [1]. Its additional content is the compatibility of these factorizations with the specified polarities and their composed polarity on the product.

Theorem 1.3.

Let ℍ⁡(UH=(AH,BH),𝔼H)\mathbb{H}(U_{H}=(A_{H},B_{H}),\mathbb{E}_{H}) and 𝕂⁡(UK=(AK,BK),𝔼K)\mathbb{K}(U_{K}=(A_{K},B_{K}),\mathbb{E}_{K}) be connected bipartite graphs that admit polarities ρH\rho_{H} and ρK\rho_{K}, with polarity quotient graphs PH​(ℍ)P_{H}(\mathbb{H}) and PK​(𝕂)P_{K}(\mathbb{K}), and let P⁡(ℍ⊙𝕂)P(\mathbb{H}\odot\mathbb{K}) be the polarity quotient graph on ℍ⊙𝕂\mathbb{H}\odot\mathbb{K} with respect to the composed polarity ρ=(ρH,ρK)\rho=(\rho_{H},\rho_{K}). Then P⁡(ℍ⊙𝕂)P(\mathbb{H}\odot\mathbb{K}) is isomorphic to PH​(ℍ)⊗PK​(𝕂).P_{H}(\mathbb{H})\otimes P_{K}(\mathbb{K}).

Corollary 5.1 then gives the polarity quotient of the entire Kronecker product:

P⁡(ℍ⊗𝕂)≅(PH​(ℍ)⊗PK​(𝕂))⊔(PH​(ℍ)⊗PK​(𝕂)).P(\mathbb{H}\otimes\mathbb{K})\cong(P_{H}(\mathbb{H})\otimes P_{K}(\mathbb{K}))\sqcup(P_{H}(\mathbb{H})\otimes P_{K}(\mathbb{K})).

In effect, Theorem 1.3 and Corollary 5.1 show that the Kronecker product is compatible with the polarity quotient on the class of bipartite graphs with polarity, as seen in Figure 1.

1.3.2. Diameter Results

The theorems and corollaries in this subsection follow from Theorem 1.3, by linking previously known inequalities on P⁡(ℍ⊙𝕂)P(\mathbb{H}\odot\mathbb{K}) and PH​(ℍ)⊗PK​(𝕂).P_{H}(\mathbb{H})\otimes P_{K}(\mathbb{K}). Theorem 1.4 gives an upper and lower bound on the diameter DD of these isomorphic graphs, in terms of the diameters of ℍ\mathbb{H} and 𝕂\mathbb{K} and diameters of their polarity quotients PH​(ℍ)P_{H}(\mathbb{H}) and PK​(𝕂)P_{K}(\mathbb{K}).

Theorem 1.4.

Let ℍ\mathbb{H} and 𝕂\mathbb{K} be as in Theorem 1.3 with diameters D⁡(ℍ)D(\mathbb{H}) and D⁡(𝕂),D(\mathbb{K}), and let their polarity quotient graphs have diameter D​(PH​(ℍ))D(P_{H}(\mathbb{H})) and D​(PK​(𝕂)).D(P_{K}(\mathbb{K})). Then the isomorphic graphs PH​(ℍ)⊗PK​(𝕂)P_{H}(\mathbb{H})\otimes P_{K}(\mathbb{K}) and P⁡(ℍ⊙𝕂)P(\mathbb{H}\odot\mathbb{K}) have diameter D,D, where

max⁡(D⁡(PH​(ℍ)),D⁡(PK​(𝕂)))≤D≤max⁡(D⁡(ℍ),D⁡(𝕂))−1.\max(D(P_{H}(\mathbb{H})),D(P_{K}(\mathbb{K})))\leq D\leq\max(D(\mathbb{H}),D(\mathbb{K}))-1.

Corollary 1.5 then gives an exact diameter for the isomorphic graphs in Theorem 1.3 when the diameters of the parent graphs and their polarity quotients differ by 11. Any pair of graphs satisfying the conditions of Corollary 1.5 may be used to obtain new graphs whose exact diameter is known. Bipartite compatibility graphs and generalized polygons both meet these conditions, and we exploit this fact to devise the new constructions in this paper.

Corollary 1.5.

Let ℍ\mathbb{H} and 𝕂\mathbb{K} be as in Theorem 1.4, where D⁡(PH​(ℍ))=D⁡(ℍ)−1D(P_{H}(\mathbb{H}))=D(\mathbb{H})-1 and D⁡(PK​(𝕂))=D⁡(𝕂)−1.D(P_{K}(\mathbb{K}))=D(\mathbb{K})-1. Then the isomorphic graphs PH​(ℍ)⊗PK​(𝕂)P_{H}(\mathbb{H})\otimes P_{K}(\mathbb{K}) and P⁡(ℍ⊙𝕂)P(\mathbb{H}\odot\mathbb{K}) have diameter max⁡(D⁡(ℍ),D⁡(𝕂))−1.\max(D(\mathbb{H}),D(\mathbb{K}))-1.

The operations here extend to an arbitrary number of bipartite graphs with polarity, so Theorems 1.3 and 1.4 can be extended to multiple such graphs.

1.3.3. Multiplicative Rule for Moore-Bound Fractions

These theorems also give a multiplicative rule for the fractions of the Moore bound approached by families of polarity quotients. Under the hypotheses of Theorem 1.6, the product has degree and order equal to the product of the factor degrees and orders, and retains the same diameter. Since MB(OPENΔ,D)∼ΔD,\Delta,D)\sim\Delta^{D}, the asymptotic Moore-bound fractions multiply when the factor degrees tend to infinity.

We note that the degree condition of Theorem 1.6 holds if and only if the polarities have non-absolute points of maximum degree. The diameter condition of Theorem 1.6 holds for graphs of equal diameter satisfying Corollary 1.5, but may hold for other families as well.

In the following theorem and throughout the paper, G¯\overline{G} denotes the graph GG with self-loops removed, giving a consistent basis for graph-order comparison with graphs in the literature.

Theorem 1.6.

Let {ℍq}\{\mathbb{H}_{q}\} and {𝕂r}\{\mathbb{K}_{r}\} be infinite families of graphs that satisfy the hypotheses of Theorem 1.3, and let 𝒫\mathcal{P} be the infinite family of graphs {PH​(ℍq)⊗PK​(𝕂r)¯}\{\overline{P_{H}(\mathbb{H}_{q})\otimes P_{K}(\mathbb{K}_{r})}\}. Let {ℍq}\{\mathbb{H}_{q}\} and {𝕂r}\{\mathbb{K}_{r}\} be such that for all admissible qq and rr,

  • •

    Δ⁡(ℍq)=Δ⁡(PH​(ℍq)¯)=ΔH,q,\Delta(\mathbb{H}_{q})=\Delta(\overline{P_{H}(\mathbb{H}_{q})})=\Delta_{H,q}, OPENΔ⁡(𝕂r)=Δ⁡(PK​(𝕂rCLOSE¯))=ΔK,r,\Delta(\mathbb{K}_{r})=\Delta(\overline{P_{K}(\mathbb{K}_{r}}))=\Delta_{K,r}, and

    D⁡(PH​(ℍq))=D⁡(PK​(𝕂r))=D⁡(PH​(ℍq)⊗PK​(𝕂r))=D.D(P_{H}(\mathbb{H}_{q}))=D(P_{K}(\mathbb{K}_{r}))=D(P_{H}(\mathbb{H}_{q})\otimes P_{K}(\mathbb{K}_{r}))=D.

Then

  1. (1)

    The graphs in 𝒫\mathcal{P} have degree ΔH,q⋅ΔK,r\Delta_{H,q}\cdot\Delta_{K,r} and diameter DD.

  2. (2)

    If the PK​(𝕂r)¯\overline{P_{K}(\mathbb{K}_{r})} approach the fraction cKc_{K} of the Moore bound as ΔK,r→∞,\Delta_{K,r}\rightarrow\infty, then the graphs in 𝒫\mathcal{P} approach the fraction fqf_{q} of the Moore bound for fixed admissible qq as ΔK,r→∞\Delta_{K,r}\rightarrow\infty, where

1.4. Paper Organization

We give basic notation and conventions in Section 2, preliminaries in Section 3, definitions and previously established theorems needed for our results in Section 4, proofs of the structural theorems in Section 5, applications of these theorems to bipartite compatibility graphs in Section 6, applications of these theorems to generalized polygons in Section 7, with a construction of a new largest graph for its degree and diameter.

2. Notation and Conventions

2.1. Notation

Throughout this paper, we use the notation in Table 1.

2.2. Kronecker Product

The Kronecker product is a common graph construction that is referred to in other papers as the direct [24, 45, 11], categorical or tensor [24] product of graphs. In [20], the term graph conjunction is used, and the term “Kronecker product” instead denotes one of the two components of the full product.

We assume that for the Kronecker product H⊗KH\otimes K, both HH and KK are connected.

In some papers, including the original Weichsel paper [46], the Kronecker product applies only to simple graphs with no self-loops. We work in the category of graphs allowing self-loops but no multiple edges, and using the definition of the Kronecker product from [24, Section 5.3]. Disallowing self-loops greatly restricts the discussion of graph homomorphisms, and in particular, the polarity quotients fundamental to this paper. These self-loops are used in the polarity constructions discussed here, giving extra edges in the Kronecker product and enabling the theorems in the paper.

2.3. Self-loops

As mentioned above, self-loops that occur in factor graphs are retained for the Kronecker product. On the other hand, the degree-diameter comparisons in the application portion of the paper make no use of self-loops, as the presence of self-loops has no effect on the diameter and order of the graph and only adds 22 to the degree of each vertex with a self-loop. Thus, after constructions are completely finished and we are comparing to the Moore bound, we delete self-loops. We then use the resulting simple graph in the comparison to compare with simple graphs from the degree-diameter literature, giving a consistent basis for comparison.

Note that the overline notation G¯\overline{G} signifies that self-loops are deleted only after the entire construction under the overline is complete.

2.4. Generalized Polygons

When we refer to the graph of a generalized nn-gon of order (s,t)(s,t), we will by default use its bipartite point-line incidence-graph representation.

2.5. Graph Order vs. Generalized-Polygon Order

The term “order” is overloaded in the concepts in this paper: the order of a graph is the number of vertices in the graph, whereas the order of a generalized polygon is a pair of parameters (s,t)(s,t) defining it. We use both definitions of order in this paper, and where needed for clarity, specify either graph or generalized-polygon order.

3. Preliminaries

3.1. The Kronecker Product and Graph Quotients

Several papers have appeared addressing quotients on the Kronecker product.

Delorme [20] devised a large-graph construction using the polarity quotient of a generalized polygon and its opposite. This is discussed in more detail in Section 3.4.2.

Jha et al. discussed graphs having a bipartition-reversing automorphism, and showed that if one of the graphs in a Kronecker product has this property, the product has two isomorphic components [29]. Hammack then showed the converse [26]. We explore this in detail for the special case of polarity, which is important in the field of finite geometry.

Hammack also studied product cancellation of factors in Kronecker products, and showed conditions on AA and BB for which A⊗C≅B⊗CA\otimes C\cong B\otimes C implies A≅BA\cong B for any CC [25]. Abay-Asmerom et al. went on to discuss Kronecker product factorization in the same context [1]. We have obtained an alternative proof of Theorem 1.3 using the factorization in [1, Proposition 1] as a starting point. However, in so doing, it is still necessary to explicitly track polarities through the factorizations of both factor graphs and their Kronecker product. The alternative proof starting with [1] thus follows the same path as the direct proof presented here, but with the actions of the polarities encoded in the factorizations, rather than explicitly described as in our proof.

The interaction of graph products and quotients was studied in a series of papers on abstract graph congruences. Broere, Heidema and Pretorius [10], Veldsman [45], and Broere, Heidema and Veldsman [11] gave graph-theoretic versions of the Isomorphism Theorems of Algebra (see e.g., [23]), and as a consequence, derive a graph-theoretic version of Birkhoff’s Subdirect Decomposition Theorem [8]:

Proposition 3.1.

[45, Theorem 2.5] [11, Theorem 2.8] Let II be an index set, and for each i∈I,i\in I, let θi\theta_{i} be a congruence on a graph GG with θ:=⋂i∈Iθi.\theta:=\bigcap\limits_{i\in I}\theta_{i}. Then G/θG/\theta is isomorphic to a subdirect product of the G/θi,G/\theta_{i}, i∈I.i\in I.

This proposition shows that the quotient is isomorphic to some unspecified subdirect product of corresponding quotient graphs. In contrast, our Theorem 1.3 shows that the quotient is the full direct product, so is more specific. Its corollary, Corollary 5.1, is also outside the scope of Proposition 3.1; P⁡(ℍ⊗𝕂)P(\mathbb{H}\otimes\mathbb{K}) gives two disjoint copies of the full direct product, so cannot be a subdirect product of these two quotient graphs.

Our theorems have an abstract flavor, like Proposition 3.1, but are entirely graph-theoretic, addressing bipartite graphs and polarity.

3.2. The Degree-Diameter Problem and the Moore Bound

Given a degree Δ\Delta and diameter DD, the degree-diameter problem of graph theory consists of finding a simple graph G⁡(Δ,D)G(\Delta,D) having largest order possible. The Moore bound [28] is a theoretical upper bound for the order of such a graph:

(1) MB​(Δ,D)=1+Δ​∑i=0D−1(Δ−1)i,\textrm{MB}(\Delta,D)=1+\Delta\sum_{i=0}^{D-1}(\Delta-1)^{i},

so when DD is fixed,

(2) limΔ→∞MB​(Δ,D)ΔD=1,\lim_{\Delta\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\textrm{MB}(\Delta,D)}{\Delta^{D}}=1,

with this immediate consequence:

Proposition 3.2.

Let {Gi}\{G_{i}\} be a family of graphs of fixed diameter DD and degree Δi→∞.\Delta_{i}\rightarrow\infty. Then

limΔi→∞|Gi|MB​(Δi,D)=c​ if and only if ​limΔi→∞|Gi|(Δi)D=c.\lim_{\Delta_{i}\rightarrow\infty}\frac{|G_{i}|}{\text{MB}(\Delta_{i},D)}=c\text{ if and only if }\lim_{\Delta_{i}\rightarrow\infty}\frac{|G_{i}|}{(\Delta_{i})^{D}}=c.

Simple graphs that reach the Moore bound are called Moore graphs. Few Moore graphs exist: these include the diameter-11 complete graphs, and the degree-22 odd cycles. There are also three diameter-22 graphs at degrees 2,32,3 and 77, and a hypothetical diameter-22 graph of degree 5757, completing the list of diameter-22 Moore graphs [28]. Damerell [18] and Bannai and Ito [6] independently proved that no Moore graphs exist with diameter D≥3D\geq 3 and degree Δ≥3\Delta\geq 3. The above list of Moore graphs is thus complete.

Many researchers have worked to improve the Moore bound; however, for all but a few special families of graphs, MB(Δ,D)−2(\Delta,D)-2 is the best currently known upper bound; see the Miller-Širáň survey [36] and the references within.

3.3. Largest Known Graphs of a Given Degree and Diameter

Since the Moore bound has proven difficult to reduce, there have been extensive efforts in constructing largest known graphs for given Δ\Delta and DD. This establishes lower bounds on the order of the largest possible graphs, and narrows the gap between the largest achieved graphs and the upper bound. Comellas provides a regularly maintained table of largest known graphs of diameters ≤10\leq 10 and degrees between 33 and 1616 at [16, 17], as a companion to his published [15]. This table is undergoing rapid change at the time of writing this paper, but in general, graphs in the table are well below 50%50\% of the Moore bound, with larger diameters usually below 10%10\%.

3.4. Known Families That Asymptotically Approach the Moore Bound

3.4.1. Generalized-Polygon Constructions Based on Polarity

Several of the largest-known graphs are based on polarities of objects in finite projective spaces.

Brown [12] and Erdös and Rényi [21] independently discovered a family of diameter-2 graphs that asymptotically achieve the Moore Bound. These are constructed by applying a polarity to the bipartite incidence graph of a finite projective plane, so these graphs exist for all degrees q+1q+1 with qq a prime power.

Delorme noted in [19] that polarity quotients of incidence graphs of certain generalized polygons asymptotically approach the Moore bound. Using generalized quadrangles, he constructed a family of diameter-3 graphs that exist for degree Δ=22​m+1+1\Delta=2^{2m+1}+1 with m∈ℤ≥0m\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}. These graphs are based on ovoids in ℙ3​(𝔽q)\mathbb{P}^{3}(\mathbb{F}_{q}), see e.g. [44, Section 7.3] for more details. For diameter 5, he constructed a similar family of graphs using generalized hexagons. This family is also sparse, and these graphs only exist for degrees Δ=32​m+1+1,\Delta=3^{2m+1}+1, m∈ℤ≥0m\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}.

In [39], Šiagiová and Širáň constructed Cayley graphs of diameter 22 and order Δ2−𝒪⁡(Δ1.5)\Delta^{2}-\mathcal{O}(\Delta^{1.5}) that approach the Moore bound. In [5], Bachratý and Širáň observed that these graphs could be constructed using polarity quotients of generalized triangles with polarity. Similarly, in [4], Bachratý, Šiagiová and Širáň constructed Cayley graphs of diameter 33 and order Δ3−𝒪⁡(Δ2.5)\Delta^{3}-\mathcal{O}(\Delta^{2.5}) that approach the Moore bound, by modifying subgraphs of the polarity quotients of generalized quadrangles with polarity. Their method does not extend to generalized hexagons.

3.4.2. Generalized-Polygon Constructions Based on Kronecker Products

Delorme constructed another family of diameter-33 graphs approaching the Moore bound in [20], based on the polarity quotient (with any self-loops removed) of the Reduced-Kronecker product of a large bipartite graph 𝔾⁡(𝕌=(𝔸,𝔹),𝔼)\mathbb{G}(\mathbb{U}=(\mathbb{A},\mathbb{B}),\mathbb{E}) and its opposite O​p​p​(𝔾)=𝔾⁡(𝕌=(𝔹,𝔸),𝔼)Opp(\mathbb{G})=\mathbb{G}(\mathbb{U}=(\mathbb{B},\mathbb{A}),\mathbb{E}), where the sets 𝔸\mathbb{A} and 𝔹\mathbb{B} are interchanged but adjacency is preserved. Large graphs are constructed when the base graph 𝔾\mathbb{G} is large: for example, Delorme used the incidence graphs of the generalized quadrangles 𝔾4​(s,t)\mathbb{G}_{4}(s,t) to construct graphs with order (1+s)​(1+t)​(1+s​t)2(1+s)(1+t)(1+st)^{2} and degree (1+s)​(1+t)(1+s)(1+t). (Generalized quadrangles exist for (s=q,t=q),(s=q−1,t=q+1),(s=q,t=q2)(s=q,t=q),(s=q-1,t=q+1),(s=q,t=q^{2}) and (s=q2,t=q3)(s=q^{2},t=q^{3}) for prime powers qq.) In [20], the second factor O​p​p​(𝔾n​(s,t))Opp(\mathbb{G}_{n}(s,t)) is determined by the first factor 𝔾n​(s,t)\mathbb{G}_{n}(s,t), unlike our construction Pm​(𝔾m)⊗Pn​(𝔾n)P_{m}(\mathbb{G}_{m})\otimes P_{n}(\mathbb{G}_{n}), where the two factors may be any pair of generalized polygons that both admit polarity. Conversely, the factors in [20] need not have a polarity. These two constructions thus produce different sets of graphs.

3.4.3. A New Construction Associated with High-Rank Spherical Buildings

Cames van Batenburg and Korsky recently introduced a family of graphs for any diameter DD that asymptotically approaches the Moore bound as the degree Δ→∞\Delta\rightarrow\infty [14]. This proves a longstanding conjecture of Bollobás [9, 13]: for every fixed D≥2D\geq 2 and every ϵ>0\epsilon>0, there are infinitely many Δ\Delta for which nD​(Δ)≥(1−ϵ)​ΔDn_{D}(\Delta)\geq(1-\epsilon)\Delta^{D}, where nD​(Δ)n_{D}(\Delta) is the largest order of a graph having diameter at most DD and maximum degree at most Δ\Delta.

This construction has as a starting point the flag geometry of the type-A2​DA_{2D} spherical building associated with V=𝔽q2​D+1V=\mathbb{F}_{q}^{2D+1}. The construction proceeds by considering the set of complete flags in VV, and splitting these flags into even and odd partial flags 𝒫e​v​e​n​(V)\mathcal{P}_{even}(V) and 𝒫o​d​d​(V)\mathcal{P}_{odd}(V). An even-rank and an odd-rank partial flag are considered compatible when their members, arranged in ascending order by rank, form a complete flag. The set 𝒫e​v​e​n​(V)\mathcal{P}_{even}(V) is the set of vertices of a graph HD,qH_{D,q}, where two even partial-flag vertices are adjacent when they share a common compatible odd partial-flag. For every fixed diameter DD, the graphs HD,qH_{D,q} have diameter DD, and the family {HD,q∣q​ a prime power}\{H_{D,q}\mid q\text{ a prime power}\} approaches the Moore bound as q→∞.q\rightarrow\infty. In fact, the authors prove a stronger variant of the Bollobás conjecture: for every fixed integer DD, limΔ→∞nD​(Δ)ΔD=1\lim_{\Delta\rightarrow\infty}\frac{n_{D}(\Delta)}{\Delta^{D}}=1.

We present in this paper a different construction, starting with the bipartite compatibility graphs that were used in [14], but then taking another line of development. We produce two families of graphs of even diameter 2​k2k, with better degree coverage.

4. Background: Products and Polarities

In this section, we present a number of definitions and propositions that are already known or that follow immediately from known propositions, along with some discussion. These are used later in the proofs of the theorems of this paper.

4.1. The Kronecker Product

Definition 4.1 (Kronecker Product of Graphs).

[46] Given two connected graphs H⁡(UH,EH)H(U_{H},E_{H}) and K⁡(UK,EK)K(U_{K},E_{K}) that permit self-loops but have no multi-edges, their Kronecker product is the graph G⁡(UH⊗UK,E)G(U_{H}\otimes U_{K},E), where ((vH,vK),(wH,wK))∈E((v_{H},v_{K}),(w_{H},w_{K}))\in E if and only if (vH,wH)∈EH(v_{H},w_{H})\in E_{H} and (vK,wK)∈EK(v_{K},w_{K})\in E_{K}. We denote this product by H⊗KH\otimes K.

Proposition 4.2.

[24] Let HH and KK be graphs. Then |V⁡(H⊗K)|=|V⁡(H)|​|V⁡(K)|.|V(H\otimes K)|=|V(H)||V(K)|.

Proposition 4.3.

[24, Proposition 5.7] Let HH and KK be graphs of diameters D⁡(H)D(H) and D⁡(K)D(K). Then max⁡(D⁡(H),D⁡(K))≤D⁡(H⊗K).\max(D(H),D(K))\leq D(H\otimes K).

Propositions 4.4 and 4.5 come from papers that define Kronecker only for loopless graphs. However, these propositions assume bipartite graphs, which must be loopless, so their Kronecker product is the same under either definition. Thus, the propositions apply in either case, and in particular, under the looped-graph Kronecker definition used here.

Proposition 4.4.

[46, Corollary of Theorem 1] Let ℍ\mathbb{H} and 𝕂\mathbb{K} be two bipartite graphs. Then their Kronecker product 𝔾=ℍ⊗𝕂\mathbb{G}=\mathbb{H}\otimes\mathbb{K} is composed of two disconnected bipartite graphs.

Proposition 4.5.

[29, Lemma 2.2] Let ℍ⁡(UH=(AH,BH),𝔼H)\mathbb{H}(U_{H}=(A_{H},B_{H}),\mathbb{E}_{H}) and 𝕂⁡(UK=(AK,BK),𝔼K)\mathbb{K}(U_{K}=(A_{K},B_{K}),\mathbb{E}_{K}) be bipartite graphs. Then the sets of vertices of the two components of ℍ⊗𝕂\mathbb{H}\otimes\mathbb{K} are (AH×AK)∪(BH×BK)(A_{H}\times A_{K})\cup(B_{H}\times B_{K}) and (AH×BK)∪(BH×AK)(A_{H}\times B_{K})\cup(B_{H}\times A_{K}).

4.2. Polarities

Definition 4.6 (Polarity).

A graph automorphism ρ\rho on a bipartite graph 𝔾⁡(U=(A,B),𝔼)\mathbb{G}(U=(A,B),\mathbb{E}) is a polarity if ρ:A→B\rho:A\rightarrow B is an involution.

The concept of polarity originates in the context of incidence graphs of finite geometries (see [20, 44] and others) and is widely discussed in that field. This was extended to the class of bipartite graphs by Lazebnik and Woldar in [32]. Hammack [25] and Abay-Asmerom et al. [1] use the terminology bipartition-reversing involution for the same concept, or just reversing involution when the bipartite context is clear. A polarity always reverses the partition of a bipartite graph, so is a special case of an involutive automorphism.

Definition 4.7 (Polarity Quotient Graph).

Let 𝔾\mathbb{G} be a bipartite graph 𝔾⁡(U=(A,B),𝔼)\mathbb{G}(U=(A,B),\mathbb{E}) and let ρ\rho be a polarity. The polarity quotient graph is the quotient graph P⁡(𝔾)P(\mathbb{G}), where vertices are the orbits of the quotient [v]={v,ρ⁡(v)}[v]=\{v,\rho(v)\} and [v][v] and [w][w] are adjacent whenever there exist v′∈[v]v^{\prime}\in[v] and w′∈[w]w^{\prime}\in[w] such that (v′,w′)∈E.(v^{\prime},w^{\prime})\in E. Multi-edges are merged into a single edge but self-loops are retained.

The notion of a polarity graph with respect to generalized polygons is well known and is discussed in [20] and elsewhere. However, in that context, self-loops are usually deleted. The quotient graph, with self-loops retained, is defined in [45, 11], and Definition 4.7 gives the quotient graph as defined in those papers, with respect to the polarity.

Definition 4.8 (Absolute Point).

An absolute point with respect to a polarity ρ\rho of a bipartite graph 𝔾\mathbb{G} is a vertex v∈V⁡(𝔾)v\in V(\mathbb{G}) such that (v,ρ⁡(v))∈E⁡(𝔾).(v,\rho(v))\in E(\mathbb{G}).

Definition 4.8 extends the terminology of finite geometry found in [44] and elsewhere to the general case of bipartite graphs. This definition, for bipartite graphs, is also seen in [32].

Definition 4.9 (Absolute Vertex of a Polarity Quotient).

An absolute vertex of a polarity quotient of a bipartite graph 𝔾\mathbb{G} is a vertex of the polarity quotient graph P⁡(𝔾)P(\mathbb{G}) resulting from the contraction of (v,ρ⁡(v))∈𝔾(v,\rho(v))\in\mathbb{G} corresponding to the orbit of {v,ρ⁡(v)}\{v,\rho(v)\} in the quotient, where vv is an absolute point. Consequently, the polarity induces a self-loop at the corresponding vertex in the quotient graph P⁡(𝔾)P(\mathbb{G}).

Proposition 4.10.

[20, Section 2] Let 𝔾\mathbb{G} be a bipartite graph (U=(A,B),𝔼)(U=(A,B),\mathbb{E}) with a polarity map ρ:A→B\rho:A\rightarrow B, and let P⁡(𝔾)¯\overline{P(\mathbb{G})} be the polarity quotient graph of 𝔾\mathbb{G} with any resulting self-loop edges dropped. Then

  1. (1)

    Δ⁡(P⁡(𝔾)¯)≤Δ⁡(𝔾)\Delta(\overline{P(\mathbb{G})})\leq\Delta(\mathbb{G}),

  2. (2)

    D⁡(P⁡(𝔾)¯)≤D⁡(𝔾)−1D(\overline{P(\mathbb{G})})\leq D(\mathbb{G})-1, and

  3. (3)

    |V(OPENP⁡(𝔾))¯|=|A|=|B|=|V⁡(𝔾)|2.|V(\overline{P(\mathbb{G}))}|=|A|=|B|=\frac{|V(\mathbb{G})|}{2}.

The following lemma is stated in [35, Theorem 2.7(i)] for the special case of generalized polygons. We generalize it to any bipartite graph with a polarity.

Lemma 4.11.

Let 𝔾\mathbb{G} be a bipartite graph with polarity ρ\rho, and let P⁡(𝔾)¯\overline{P(\mathbb{G})} be the polarity quotient graph of 𝔾\mathbb{G} with self-loop edges dropped. Then Δ⁡(P⁡(𝔾)¯)=Δ⁡(𝔾)\Delta(\overline{P(\mathbb{G})})=\Delta(\mathbb{G}) if and only if there exist points in 𝔾\mathbb{G} of maximal degree that are not absolute with respect to ρ.\rho.

Proof.

Let vv be a vertex of GG. Since ρ\rho is an automorphism, each edge (v,w)(v,w) induces an edge ([v],[w])([v],[w]) in P⁡(G)P(G). These edges are distinct: since GG is bipartite and ρ\rho is a polarity, no more than one of ww and ρ⁡(w)\rho(w) can be a neighbor of vv. Thus, the number of edges incident to [v][v] is equal to the degree of vv. If vv is absolute with respect to ρ\rho, then [v][v] has a self-loop deleted in P⁡(G)P(G), i.e., one fewer edge incident to [v][v]. All remaining edges join [v][v] and a neighbor in P⁡(G)P(G), so in this case, [v][v] will have degree deg(v)−1(v)-1 in P⁡(G)P(G). So vertices [v][v] from absolute points vv have degree 11 smaller than vv, completing the proof. ∎

4.3. Bipartition-Reversing Automorphisms and Kronecker Products

An automorphism on a bipartite graph must either reverse or preserve its partitions [1]. In [29], Jha et al. gave several results on Kronecker products of bipartite graphs that have a reversing automorphism, i.e., that exchanges the partitions. We will use their results to show theorems on Kronecker products of bipartite graphs that admit polarity, enabling the main theoretical results of this paper.

We recall from Section 2.3 that any self-loops that emerge during construction are retained until we conduct degree/diameter comparisons to other graphs at the end of the construction, at which point we drop the self-loops.

Definition 4.12 (Bipartition-Reversing Automorphism).

[29, Definition 3.1] [1, Page 2043] A bipartite graph 𝔾=(U=(A,B),𝔼)\mathbb{G}=(U=(A,B),\mathbb{E}) has a bipartition-reversing automorphism when 𝔾\mathbb{G} admits an automorphism ψ:A→B\psi:A\rightarrow B. (In [29], a graph having such an automorphism is said to have Property π\pi.)

A bipartition-reversing automorphism is called a duality when discussing incidence graphs of finite geometries [19, 20, 44]. The theorems of Section 5 apply to bipartite graphs, but one of our applications is from finite geometry, so we mention duality here for context.

The forward implication of Theorem 4.13 was shown by Jha et al. in 1997 [29]. The converse remained a conjecture until Hammack proved it in 2009 [26].

Theorem 4.13.

[29, Theorem 3.2] [26, Theorem 1] Let ℍ\mathbb{H} and 𝕂\mathbb{K} be bipartite graphs. The two components of ℍ⊗𝕂\mathbb{H}\otimes\mathbb{K} are isomorphic if and only if at least one of ℍ\mathbb{H} and 𝕂\mathbb{K} has a bipartition-reversing automorphism.

Definition 4.14 (Reduced-Kronecker product of graphs).

[29, 26] Let ℍ\mathbb{H} and 𝕂\mathbb{K} be bipartite graphs, at least one of which has a bipartition-reversing automorphism. Their Reduced-Kronecker product ℍ⊙𝕂\mathbb{H}\odot\mathbb{K} is one of the two components of their Kronecker product ℍ⊗𝕂\mathbb{H}\otimes\mathbb{K}, which by Theorem 4.13 are isomorphic.

Proposition 4.15(2)(2) is due to Puš [38, Corollary 1], who attributes it to Hell [27]. Propositions 4.15(1)(1) and (3)(3) follow directly from Theorem 4.13 and Proposition 4.5 of [29], and the definition of Kronecker product.

Proposition 4.15.

Let ℍ⁡(UH=(AH,BH),𝔼H)\mathbb{H}(U_{H}=(A_{H},B_{H}),\mathbb{E}_{H}) and 𝕂⁡(UK=(AK,BK),𝔼K)\mathbb{K}(U_{K}=(A_{K},B_{K}),\mathbb{E}_{K}) be connected bipartite graphs, at least one of which has a bipartition-reversing automorphism. Then the degree Δ\Delta, diameter DD and number of vertices |V⁡(𝔾)||V(\mathbb{G})| of the Reduced-Kronecker product 𝔾=ℍ⊙𝕂\mathbb{G}=\mathbb{H}\odot\mathbb{K} are

  1. (1)

    Δ⁡(𝔾)=Δ⁡(ℍ)​Δ​(𝕂),\Delta(\mathbb{G})=\Delta(\mathbb{H})\Delta(\mathbb{K}),

  2. (2)

    D⁡(𝔾)=max⁡(D⁡(ℍ),D⁡(𝕂)),D(\mathbb{G})=\max(D(\mathbb{H}),D(\mathbb{K})), and

  3. (3)

    |V⁡(𝔾)|=|AH|​|AK|+|BH|​|BK|.|V(\mathbb{G})|=|A_{H}||A_{K}|+|B_{H}||B_{K}|.

Proposition 4.16.

[29, Proposition 3.3] Let ℍ\mathbb{H} and 𝕂\mathbb{K} be bipartite graphs having bipartition-reversing automorphisms ρH\rho_{H} and ρK\rho_{K}. Then the isomorphic components of ℍ⊗𝕂\mathbb{H}\otimes\mathbb{K} also have a bipartition-reversing automorphism ρ⁡((h,k))=(ρH​(h),ρK​(k))\rho((h,k))=(\rho_{H}(h),\rho_{K}(k)).

4.4. Polarities and Kronecker Products

A polarity is a bipartition-reversing automorphism, so any theorem regarding graphs with bipartition-reversing automorphisms also holds for graphs admitting polarity. Corollary 4.17 then follows immediately from Proposition 4.16, since the automorphism on ℍ⊙𝕂\mathbb{H}\odot\mathbb{K} will be an involution, as will that on ℍ⊗𝕂\mathbb{H}\otimes\mathbb{K}.

Corollary 4.17.

Let ℍ\mathbb{H} and 𝕂\mathbb{K} be bipartite graphs that admit polarity. Then both ℍ⊗𝕂\mathbb{H}\otimes\mathbb{K} and ℍ⊙𝕂\mathbb{H}\odot\mathbb{K} admit polarity, with the polarity ρ\rho as in Proposition 4.16.

Definition 4.18 (Composed Polarity).

Let ℍ\mathbb{H} and 𝕂\mathbb{K} be bipartite graphs with polarities ρH\rho_{H} and ρK\rho_{K}. The composed polarity ρ\rho on ℍ⊗𝕂\mathbb{H}\otimes\mathbb{K} and on ℍ⊙𝕂\mathbb{H}\odot\mathbb{K} is the map ρ⁡((h,k))=(ρH​(h),ρK​(k)).\rho((h,k))=(\rho_{H}(h),\rho_{K}(k)).

We observe that when ℍ\mathbb{H} and 𝕂\mathbb{K} are bipartite graphs admitting polarity, ℍ⊗𝕂\mathbb{H}\otimes\mathbb{K} admits other polarities beyond the composed polarity ρ\rho. Let γ\gamma be an isomorphism from one component of ℍ⊗𝕂\mathbb{H}\otimes\mathbb{K} to the other. Any automorphism ψ\psi of ℍ⊙𝕂\mathbb{H}\odot\mathbb{K} induces an isomorphism ϕγ,ψ≠ρ:ϕγ,ψ​(v)=ψ⁡(γ⁡(v))\phi_{\gamma,\psi}\neq\rho:\phi_{\gamma,\psi}(v)=\psi(\gamma(v)), sending one component of ℍ⊗𝕂\mathbb{H}\otimes\mathbb{K} onto the other, using ψ\psi in one direction and ψ−1\psi^{-1} in the other. It is therefore a polarity of ℍ⊗𝕂\mathbb{H}\otimes\mathbb{K} arising from one of its two bipartitions. The polarity quotient of ϕγ,ψ\phi_{\gamma,\psi} is isomorphic to ℍ⊙𝕂,\mathbb{H}\odot\mathbb{K}, so differs from the polarity quotient of ρ\rho (discussed in Corollary 5.1 of Theorem 1.3).

Different polarities on isomorphic graphs may yield nonisomorphic polarity quotients with the same maximum degree, diameter and order; examples of this are given in Table 3. We limit our discussion to the composed polarity ρ\rho for the rest of this paper, since this polarity leads to the structural and degree-diameter results in this paper.

Proof.

Let 𝔾1\mathbb{G}_{1} and 𝔾2\mathbb{G}_{2} be the isomorphic components of ℍ⊗𝕂.\mathbb{H}\otimes\mathbb{K}. By Corollary 4.17, the composed polarity ρ\rho restricts to a polarity on each isomorphic component of ℍ⊗𝕂\mathbb{H}\otimes\mathbb{K}, so we may apply Theorem 1.3 to either component of ℍ⊗𝕂\mathbb{H}\otimes\mathbb{K}:

P⁡(ℍ⊗𝕂)=P⁡(𝔾1⊔𝔾2)=P⁡(𝔾1)⊔P⁡(𝔾2)≅(PH​(ℍ)⊗PK​(𝕂))⊔(PH​(ℍ)⊗PK​(𝕂)).P(\mathbb{H}\otimes\mathbb{K})=P(\mathbb{G}_{1}\sqcup\mathbb{G}_{2})=P(\mathbb{G}_{1})\sqcup P(\mathbb{G}_{2})\cong(P_{H}(\mathbb{H})\otimes P_{K}(\mathbb{K}))\sqcup(P_{H}(\mathbb{H})\otimes P_{K}(\mathbb{K})).

∎

Lemma 5.2.

Let ℍ\mathbb{H} and 𝕂\mathbb{K} be bipartite graphs admitting polarity with diameters D⁡(ℍ)D(\mathbb{H}) and D⁡(𝕂)D(\mathbb{K}) and let P⁡(ℍ⊙𝕂)P(\mathbb{H}\odot\mathbb{K}) be the composed-polarity quotient on ℍ⊙𝕂.\mathbb{H}\odot\mathbb{K}. Then

D⁡(P⁡(ℍ⊙𝕂))≤max⁡(D⁡(ℍ),D⁡(𝕂))−1.D(P(\mathbb{H}\odot\mathbb{K}))\leq\max(D(\mathbb{H}),D(\mathbb{K}))-1.
Proof.

By Corollary 4.17, ℍ⊙𝕂\mathbb{H}\odot\mathbb{K} admits polarity, so has a bipartition-reversing automorphism. So by Proposition 4.15(2)(2), D⁡(ℍ⊙𝕂)−1=max⁡(D⁡(ℍ),D⁡(𝕂))−1.D(\mathbb{H}\odot\mathbb{K})-1=\max(D(\mathbb{H}),D(\mathbb{K}))-1. By Proposition 4.4 and the definition of the Reduced-Kronecker product, ℍ⊙𝕂\mathbb{H}\odot\mathbb{K} is bipartite, so by Proposition 4.10(2)(2), D⁡(P⁡(ℍ⊙𝕂))≤D⁡(ℍ⊙𝕂)−1=max⁡(D⁡(ℍ),D⁡(𝕂))−1.D(P(\mathbb{H}\odot\mathbb{K}))\leq D(\mathbb{H}\odot\mathbb{K})-1=\max(D(\mathbb{H}),D(\mathbb{K}))-1. ∎

Theorem 1.4 and Corollary 1.5 follow quickly from the preceding results.

Proof of Theorem 1.4.

P⁡(ℍ⊙𝕂)≅PH​(ℍ)⊗PK​(𝕂)P(\mathbb{H}\odot\mathbb{K})\cong P_{H}(\mathbb{H})\otimes P_{K}(\mathbb{K}) by Theorem 1.3, so this follows from Proposition 4.3 and Lemma 5.2. ∎

Proof of Corollary 1.5.

Follows from Theorem 1.4:

max⁡(D⁡(PH​(ℍ)),D⁡(PK​(𝕂)))=max⁡(D⁡(ℍ),D⁡(𝕂))−1.\max(D(P_{H}(\mathbb{H})),D(P_{K}(\mathbb{K})))=\max(D(\mathbb{H}),D(\mathbb{K}))-1.

∎

Proof of Theorem 1.6.

The order of PH​(ℍq)⊗PK​(𝕂r)P_{H}(\mathbb{H}_{q})\otimes P_{K}(\mathbb{K}_{r}) is |PH​(ℍq)|⋅|PK​(𝕂r)|,|P_{H}(\mathbb{H}_{q})|\cdot|P_{K}(\mathbb{K}_{r})|, by the definition of the Kronecker product. Lemma 4.11, Proposition 4.15 and the condition on degrees give that the degrees of the graphs in 𝒫\mathcal{P} are ΔH,q⋅ΔK,r\Delta_{H,q}\cdot\Delta_{K,r}. By Theorem 1.3 and the diameter condition, diameter is DD for all graphs in these families. We expand the Moore bound ratio:

|PH​(ℍq)|⋅|PK​(𝕂r)|M​B​(ΔH,q⋅ΔK,r,D)=|PK​(𝕂r)|(ΔK,r)D⋅|PH​(ℍq)|(ΔH,q)D⋅(ΔH,q⋅ΔK,r)DM​B​(ΔH,q⋅ΔK,r,D)\frac{|P_{H}(\mathbb{H}_{q})|\cdot|P_{K}(\mathbb{K}_{r})|}{MB(\Delta_{H,q}\cdot\Delta_{K,r},D)}=\frac{|P_{K}(\mathbb{K}_{r})|}{(\Delta_{K,r})^{D}}\cdot\frac{|P_{H}(\mathbb{H}_{q})|}{(\Delta_{H,q})^{D}}\cdot\frac{(\Delta_{H,q}\cdot\Delta_{K,r})^{D}}{MB(\Delta_{H,q}\cdot\Delta_{K,r},D)}

If qq and thus ΔH,q\Delta_{H,q} are held fixed, we apply Proposition 3.2 and Equation (2) to get

fq\displaystyle f_{q} =limΔK,r→∞(|PK​(𝕂r)|(ΔK,r)D⋅|PH​(ℍq)|(ΔH,q)D⋅(ΔH,q⋅ΔK,r)DM​B​(ΔH,q⋅ΔK,r,D))\displaystyle=\lim_{\Delta_{K,r}\rightarrow\infty}\left(\frac{|P_{K}(\mathbb{K}_{r})|}{(\Delta_{K,r})^{D}}\cdot\frac{|P_{H}(\mathbb{H}_{q})|}{(\Delta_{H,q})^{D}}\cdot\frac{(\Delta_{H,q}\cdot\Delta_{K,r})^{D}}{MB(\Delta_{H,q}\cdot\Delta_{K,r},D)}\right)
=cK⋅|PH​(ℍq)|(ΔH,q)D\displaystyle=c_{K}\cdot\frac{|P_{H}(\mathbb{H}_{q})|}{(\Delta_{H,q})^{D}}

If both ΔH,q,ΔK,r→∞,\Delta_{H,q},\Delta_{K,r}\rightarrow\infty, we apply Proposition 3.2 twice and Equation (2) once to get

f\displaystyle f =limΔH,q,ΔK,r→∞(|PK​(𝕂r)|(ΔK,r)D⋅|PH​(ℍq)|(ΔH,q)D⋅(ΔH,q⋅ΔK,r)DM​B​(ΔH,q⋅ΔK,r,D))\displaystyle=\lim_{\Delta_{H,q},\Delta_{K,r}\rightarrow\infty}\left(\frac{|P_{K}(\mathbb{K}_{r})|}{(\Delta_{K,r})^{D}}\cdot\frac{|P_{H}(\mathbb{H}_{q})|}{(\Delta_{H,q})^{D}}\cdot\frac{(\Delta_{H,q}\cdot\Delta_{K,r})^{D}}{MB(\Delta_{H,q}\cdot\Delta_{K,r},D)}\right)
=cK⋅cH.\displaystyle=c_{K}\cdot c_{H}.

∎

5.2. Applications

Any pair of graphs that satisfy the conditions of Corollary 1.5 may be used in the construction here to obtain new graphs whose exact diameter is known. Many examples of such graphs may be constructed: for example, the family of ladder graphs LnL_{n} with the rail interchange polarity has this property, as does the family of graphs made by attaching two copies of the star graph K1,n,n≥2,K_{1,n},n\geq 2, by an edge joining the center vertices with the pair-branch interchange polarity.

We discuss in the following sections two important examples of graphs of this type: the bipartite compatibility graphs and the generalized nn-gons that admit polarity. The polarity quotient graphs of each of these families reach the Moore bound asymptotically, as do Kronecker products of these polarity quotients when the factors have the same fixed diameter and both degrees tend to infinity.

6. Structural Results Applied to High-Rank Spherical Buildings

Here, we apply the results from Section 5 to the special case of flag geometries of high-rank spherical buildings to construct new families of large graphs. This construction takes as a starting point the bipartite compatibility graph construction ℂ⁡(k,q)\mathbb{C}(k,q) appearing as the initial idea in [14]. The ℂ⁡(k,q)\mathbb{C}(k,q) are constructed using the odd- and even-dimensional partial flags from the spherical building of type A2​kA_{2k} associated with 𝔽q2​k+1\mathbb{F}_{q}^{2k+1} [2, Section 4.3]. In [14], the authors use these to construct infinite families of graphs of any diameter kk and degree ∼(q+1)2​k\sim(q+1)^{2k} that approach the Moore bound.

Our construction proceeds along different lines from the halved-flag construction in [14]. We first establish a natural polarity on the bipartite compatibility graphs. This polarity produces a family of graphs of even diameter 2​k2k and of degree Δq=(q+1)k\Delta_{q}=(q+1)^{k}, with qq a prime power, that approaches the Moore bound asymptotically as the degrees Δq→∞.\Delta_{q}\rightarrow\infty.

We also find that these graphs with their natural polarity satisfy the conditions of the theorems and corollaries in Section 5, so we may construct Kronecker products of these graphs having the same diameter. This gives a second family of graphs of even diameter 2​k2k and of degree Δq,r=[(q+1)​(r+1)]k\Delta_{q,r}=[(q+1)(r+1)]^{k}, with q,rq,r prime powers, that approaches the Moore bound asymptotically as the degrees Δq,Δr→∞.\Delta_{q},\Delta_{r}\rightarrow\infty.

We note that the graphs ℂ⁡(1,q)\mathbb{C}(1,q) are isomorphic to the incidence graphs of the Desarguesian generalized triangles P​G​(2,q)PG(2,q), which are rank-22 spherical buildings of type A2A_{2} [2, Section 0.5]. The Erdős-Rényi-Brown polarity graphs are polarity quotients of the incidence graphs of these buildings [21, 12], thus the constructions in this section generalize the classical Erdős-Rényi–Brown polarity construction to higher rank.

We do not consider this case k=1k=1 further in this section, but assume that k>1k>1 when discussing the ℂ⁡(k,q)\mathbb{C}(k,q) constructions. We discuss these generalized triangles in more detail in Section 7, in the context of generalized polygons.

6.1. Some Preliminaries

Definition 6.1 (Flag, Complete Flag).

[40, page 101 (1.114)] Let VV be a tt-dimensional vector space. A flag in VV is an increasing chain of subspaces of V,V, F=(W1⊂⋯⊂Wm).F=(W_{1}\subset\dots\subset W_{m}). A complete flag in VV is a flag with a subspace of every dimension from 00 to tt.

Definition 6.2 (Orthogonal Complement of a Flag).

[41, Equations 7.8, 7.9] Let V=𝔽q2​k+1,V=\mathbb{F}_{q}^{2k+1}, where qq is a prime power and k∈ℤ>0,k\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}, and let F=(W1⊂⋯⊂Wm)F=(W_{1}\subset\dots\subset W_{m}) be some flag on VV. Let BB be a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form on VV. The orthogonal complement of the flag FF with respect to BB is the chain F⟂=(Wm⟂,…,W1⟂),F^{\perp}=(W_{m}^{\perp},\dots,W_{1}^{\perp}), where Wi⟂W_{i}^{\perp} is the set of all vectors of VV orthogonal to WiW_{i} with respect to BB.

Definition 6.3 (qq-Integer tt, qq-Factorial of tt).

[40] The qq-integer tt (qq analogue of tt) is

[t]q=1+q+⋯+qt−1=qt−1q−1=|P​G​(t−1,q)|.[t]_{q}=1+q+\dots+q^{t-1}=\frac{q^{t}-1}{q-1}=|PG(t-1,q)|.

The qq-factorial of tt (qq analogue of t!t!) is

[t]q!=1​(1+q)​…​(1+q+⋯+qt−1)=∏j=1t[j]q.[t]_{q}!=1(1+q)\dots(1+q+\dots+q^{t-1})=\prod_{j=1}^{t}[j]_{q}.
Proposition 6.4.

[40, Proposition 1.10.12] Let VV be a tt-dimensional vector space over 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}. Then the number of complete flags in VV is [t]q!.[t]_{q}!.

6.2. The Bipartite Compatibility Graph

This graph, which we denote by ℂ⁡(k,q)\mathbb{C}(k,q), is defined in [14]. The bipartite compatibility graph is the starting point for both Hk,qH_{k,q} construction in  [14] and our construction. Beyond that, both constructions are different.

Partial flags of some rank set SS are maximal chains in an SS-rank-selected subposet of PP, where PP is the lattice of subspaces of VV, ordered by inclusion and ranked by dimension (see [40, Section 3.13]). In [14], Cames van Batenburg and Korsky distinguish these particular flags and refer to them as odd-/even-rank partial flags. We use the definition from [14], except that we include {0}\{0\} and VV as flag elements.

Definition 6.5 (Partial Flags of Odd-/Even-Rank Type).

[14] Let VV be a tt-dimensional vector space, where ℱ⁡(V)\mathcal{F}(V) is the set of complete flags on VV. We define

Fo​d​d=(Wi)0≤i≤ti​odd, and ​Fe​v​e​n=(Wi)0≤i≤ti​e​v​e​n.F_{odd}=(W_{i})_{\begin{subarray}{c}0\leq i\leq t\\ i\ \mathrm{odd}\end{subarray}},\text{ and }F_{even}=(W_{i})_{\begin{subarray}{c}0\leq i\leq t\\ i\ even\end{subarray}}.

Then the set of partial flags of odd-rank type in VV is 𝒫o​d​d​(V)={Fo​d​d:F∈ℱ⁡(V)}\mathcal{P}_{odd}(V)=\{F_{odd}:F\in\mathcal{F}(V)\} and the set of partial flags of even-rank type in VV is 𝒫e​v​e​n​(V)={Fe​v​e​n:F∈ℱ⁡(V)}.\mathcal{P}_{even}(V)=\{F_{even}:F\in\mathcal{F}(V)\}.

Definition 6.6 (Compatible Flags).

[14] An odd flag Fo​d​dF_{odd} and an even flag Fe​v​e​nF_{even} of VV are said to be compatible if when interleaved by rank, they produce a complete flag on VV.

Definition 6.7 (Bipartite Compatibility Graph).

[14] Let V=𝔽q2​k+1,V=\mathbb{F}_{q}^{2k+1}, where qq is a prime power and k∈ℤ>0.k\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}. The bipartite compatibility graph of VV is the bipartite graph with vertex set 𝒫o​d​d​(V)⊔𝒫e​v​e​n​(V)\mathcal{P}_{odd}(V)\sqcup\mathcal{P}_{even}(V), and edges (Fa,Fb)(F_{a},F_{b}) when Fa∈𝒫o​d​d​(V)F_{a}\in\mathcal{P}_{odd}(V), Fb∈𝒫e​v​e​n​(V)F_{b}\in\mathcal{P}_{even}(V) and FaF_{a} and FbF_{b} are compatible. We denote this graph by ℂ⁡(k,q).\mathbb{C}(k,q).

Proposition 6.8 follows immediately from the definitions above and Proposition 6.4. Cames van Batenburg and Korsky also make these arguments in [14, Proposition 3.1].

Proposition 6.8.

The graph ℂ⁡(k,q)\mathbb{C}(k,q) is (q+1)k(q+1)^{k}-regular, and in particular, Δ⁡(ℂ⁡(k,q))=(q+1)k.\Delta(\mathbb{C}(k,q))=(q+1)^{k}. Its order is 2​[2​k+1]q!(q+1)k.\frac{2[2k+1]_{q}!}{(q+1)^{k}}.

Proof.

Let Fe​v​e​n=({0}=W0⊂⋯⊂W2​k)F_{even}=(\{0\}=W_{0}\subset\dots\subset W_{2k}) be a partial flag of even-rank type and let Fo​d​d=(W1⊂⋯⊂W2​k+1=V).F_{odd}=(W_{1}\subset\dots\subset W_{2k+1}=V). Fo​d​dF_{odd} is compatible with Fe​v​e​nF_{even} if and only if W2​i⊊W2​i+1⊊W2​i+2,W_{2i}\subsetneq W_{2i+1}\subsetneq W_{2i+2}, for all 0≤i≤k−1.0\leq i\leq k-1. For each ii, the quotient W2​i+2/W2​iW_{2i+2}/W_{2i} has dimension 22, so the possible W2​i+1W_{2i+1} correspond to the 11-dimensional spaces in the quotient. There are q+1q+1 of these, so there must be (q+1)k(q+1)^{k} independent choices for Fo​d​dF_{odd}, so each element of 𝒫e​v​e​n​(V)\mathcal{P}_{even}(V) has degree (q+1)k.(q+1)^{k}. By a similar argument, each element of 𝒫o​d​d​(V)\mathcal{P}_{odd}(V) has degree (q+1)k.(q+1)^{k}. So ℂ⁡(k,q)\mathbb{C}(k,q) is (q+1)k(q+1)^{k}-regular.

The number of edges in ℂ⁡(k,q)\mathbb{C}(k,q) is the same as the number of complete flags in VV, and by Proposition 6.4, the number of complete flags in VV is [2​k+1]q![2k+1]_{q}! Since ℂ⁡(k,q)\mathbb{C}(k,q) is (q+1)k(q+1)^{k}-regular, the degree-sum formula gives |ℂ⁡(k,q)|=2​[2​k+1]q!(q+1)k.|\mathbb{C}(k,q)|=\frac{2[2k+1]_{q}!}{(q+1)^{k}}. ∎

Definition 6.9 (Rank Function).

[14] Let FF be a flag in VV and let e∈V.e\in V. The rank function is the largest rank of any subspace in FF not containing ee (and 00 if every member of FF contains ee):

λ(e,F)=max({dimW:W∈F,e∉W}∪{0}).\lambda(e,F)=\max(\{\dim W:W\in F,e\notin W\}\cup\{0\}).
Lemma 6.10.

[14, adapted from proof of Proposition 3.1] Let F,F′∈ℂ⁡(k,q),F,F^{\prime}\in\mathbb{C}(k,q), and let λ\lambda be the rank function of Definition 6.9. If λ⁡(e,F)=d1\lambda(e,F)=d_{1} and λ⁡(e,F′)=d2\lambda(e,F^{\prime})=d_{2} for some e∈V,e\in V, then the shortest path between FF and F′F^{\prime} in ℂ⁡(k,q)\mathbb{C}(k,q) has length at least |d1−d2|.\lvert d_{1}-d_{2}\rvert.

Proof.

If FF and F′F^{\prime} are adjacent in ℂ⁡(k,q)\mathbb{C}(k,q), interleaving their subspaces gives a complete flag (0=W0⊂W1⊂…⊂W2​k+1=V).({0}=W_{0}\subset W_{1}\subset\ldots\subset W_{2k+1}=V). For any e∈Ve\in V, let dd be the smallest dimension such that e∈Wde\in W_{d}. Since dd is smallest, e∉Wie\notin W_{i} for i<di<d and since subspaces in a complete flag are nested, e∈Wie\in W_{i} for i≥di\geq d. So for any ee, |λ⁡(e,F)−λ⁡(e,F′)|≤1.\lvert\lambda(e,F)-\lambda(e,F^{\prime})\rvert\leq 1. Let F=F0,F1,…,Fm=F′F=F_{0},F_{1},\dots,F_{m}=F^{\prime} be a path of length mm between FF and F′.F^{\prime}. Then by the triangle inequality, |d1−d2|≤∑i=1m|λ⁡(e,Fi−1)−λ⁡(e,Fi)|≤m.\lvert d_{1}-d_{2}\rvert\leq\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lvert\lambda(e,F_{i-1})-\lambda(e,F_{i})\rvert\leq m. ∎

Theorem 6.11.

Let V=𝔽q2​k+1,V=\mathbb{F}_{q}^{2k+1}, where qq is a prime power and k∈ℤ>0k\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0} and let ℂ⁡(k,q)\mathbb{C}(k,q) be the bipartite compatibility graph on VV. Then the diameter of ℂ⁡(k,q)\mathbb{C}(k,q) is 2​k+12k+1.

Proof.

For the upper bound in this proof, we reproduce the argument in [14, Lemma 2.1]. It is a standard fact (see e.g. [2, proof of Axiom B1]) that any two complete flags FF and F′F^{\prime} are induced by two orderings of a common basis {e1,…,e2​k+1},\{e_{1},\dots,e_{2k+1}\}, where Wi=span​(e1,…,ei)W_{i}=\text{span}(e_{1},\dots,e_{i}) and Wi′=span​(eπ⁡(1),…,eπ⁡(i)),W_{i}^{\prime}=\text{span}(e_{\pi(1)},\dots,e_{\pi(i)}), where 1≤i≤2​k+11\leq i\leq 2k+1 and π∈S2​k+1.\pi\in S_{2k+1}. Applying odd-even sorting to π\pi, as in [3, Section 22], gives a route between FF and F′F^{\prime} that changes only even-rank subspaces on even steps and only odd-rank subspaces on odd steps, so this route provides a path between Fe​v​e​nF_{even} and Fo​d​d′F_{odd}^{\prime} of length at most 2​k+12k+1. The same argument gives a path of length at most 2​k2k between Fo​d​dF_{odd} and Fo​d​d′F_{odd}^{\prime} and between Fe​v​e​nF_{even} and Fe​v​e​n′,F_{even}^{\prime}, so D⁡(ℂ⁡(k,q))≤2​k+1.D(\mathbb{C}(k,q))\leq 2k+1.

We now extend the result from [14] by finding the exact diameter. Let e≠0e\neq 0 and let Fo​d​d′F_{odd}^{\prime} be an odd partial flag (⟨e⟩⊂⋯⊂V)(\langle e\rangle\subset\dots\subset V) and let Fe​v​e​nF_{even} be an even partial flag ({0}⊂⋯⊂W),(\{0\}\subset\dots\subset W), where V=W⊕⟨e⟩.V=W\oplus\langle e\rangle. Clearly, λ⁡(e,Fe​v​e​n)=2​k\lambda(e,F_{even})=2k and λ⁡(e,Fo​d​d′)=0\lambda(e,F_{odd}^{\prime})=0. Then by Lemma 6.10, the shortest path between Fo​d​d′F_{odd}^{\prime} and Fe​v​e​nF_{even} has length at least 2​k.2k. However, Fe​v​e​nF_{even} and Fo​d​d′F_{odd}^{\prime} are on the opposite sides of the bipartite ℂ⁡(k,q)\mathbb{C}(k,q) so any path between them must have an odd number of edges. So D⁡(ℂ⁡(k,q))≥2​k+1,D(\mathbb{C}(k,q))\geq 2k+1, and this, with the upper bound, gives D⁡(ℂ⁡(k,q))=2​k+1.D(\mathbb{C}(k,q))=2k+1. ∎

6.3. Polarity on the Bipartite Compatibility Graph

In this section, we show a natural polarity on the bipartite compatibility graph.

Lemma 6.12.

Let V=𝔽q2​k+1,V=\mathbb{F}_{q}^{2k+1}, where qq is a prime power and k∈ℤ>0,k\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}, let F=(W1⊂⋯⊂Wm)F=(W_{1}\subset\dots\subset W_{m}) be a flag on VV, and let BB be a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form on VV. Then F⟂=(Wm⟂⊂⋯⊂W1⟂)F^{\perp}=(W_{m}^{\perp}\subset\dots\subset W_{1}^{\perp}) is also a flag on VV, where Wi⟂W_{i}^{\perp} is the set of all vectors in VV that are orthogonal to WiW_{i} with respect to BB. Moreover, FF is a complete flag if and only if F⟂F^{\perp} is a complete flag, and FF is a flag of even-rank type if and only if F⟂F^{\perp} is a flag of odd-rank type.

Proof.

Let WiW_{i} and WjW_{j} be subspaces occurring in F,F, where Wi⊂Wj.W_{i}\subset W_{j}. Then Wi⟂W_{i}^{\perp} and Wj⟂W_{j}^{\perp} are in F⟂F^{\perp} and Wj⟂⊆Wi⟂.W_{j}^{\perp}\subseteq W_{i}^{\perp}. BB is nondegenerate, so the dimension of Wj⟂W_{j}^{\perp} is 2​k+1−dimWj,2k+1-\dim W_{j}, and the dimension of Wi⟂W_{i}^{\perp} is 2​k+1−dimWi.2k+1-\dim W_{i}. So the inclusion is proper and Wj⟂⊂Wi⟂.W_{j}^{\perp}\subset W_{i}^{\perp}. A flag FF is complete if and only if FF contains subspaces of every dimension ≤2​k+1,\leq 2k+1, if and only if F⟂F^{\perp} contains subspaces of every dimension ≤2​k+1,\leq 2k+1, if and only if F⟂F^{\perp} is a complete flag. Finally WiW_{i} has even dimension if and only if Wi⟂W_{i}^{\perp} has odd dimension, so the orthogonal complement interchanges partial flags of odd-rank type and partial flags of even-rank type. ∎

Theorem 6.13.

Let V=𝔽q2​k+1,V=\mathbb{F}_{q}^{2k+1}, where qq is a prime power and k∈ℤ>0.k\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}. Let BB be a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form on VV and let ℂ⁡(k,q)\mathbb{C}(k,q) be the bipartite compatibility graph on VV. Then the orthogonal-complement mapping on the vertices of ℂ⁡(k,q)\mathbb{C}(k,q) with respect to BB is a polarity.

Proof.

The orthogonal complement of a flag is an involution. VV is of odd dimension, so the orthogonal complement of an odd-dimensional subspace WiW_{i} has even dimension 2​k+1−i2k+1-i, and vice versa. The orthogonal complement is thus a bijective mapping interchanging the partitions 𝒫o​d​d​(V)\mathcal{P}_{odd}(V) and 𝒫e​v​e​n​(V)\mathcal{P}_{even}(V) of ℂ⁡(k,q)\mathbb{C}(k,q). So the orthogonal complement is a bipartition-swapping involution. Let FF be a complete flag on VV, where Fo​d​dF_{odd} is its partial subflag of odd-rank type and Fe​v​e​nF_{even} is its partial subflag of even-rank type. By Lemma 6.12, F⟂F^{\perp}, the orthogonal complement of FF, is also a complete flag. Under orthogonal complementation,

Fo​d​d→(Fo​d​d)⟂=(F⟂)e​v​e​nF_{odd}\rightarrow(F_{odd})^{\perp}=(F^{\perp})_{even}

and

Fe​v​e​n→(Fe​v​e​n)⟂=(F⟂)o​d​d.F_{even}\rightarrow(F_{even})^{\perp}=(F^{\perp})_{odd}.

So orthogonal complementation on ℂ⁡(k,q)\mathbb{C}(k,q) preserves edges, so is an automorphism. ∎

Definition 6.14 (Orthogonal-Complement Polarity and Quotient Graph).

The orthogonal-complement polarity β\beta on ℂ⁡(k,q)\mathbb{C}(k,q) is the orthogonal-complement mapping with respect to BB on the vertices of ℂ⁡(k,q)\mathbb{C}(k,q), i.e., the partial flags of even- and odd-rank type. The polarity quotient graph of ℂ⁡(k,q)\mathbb{C}(k,q) with respect to β\beta is denoted by Pβ​(ℂ​(k,q)).P_{\beta}(\mathbb{C}(k,q)).

Theorem 6.15.

7. Structural Results Applied to Generalized Polygons

Here, we apply the results from Section 5 to the special case of generalized polygons to construct new families of large graphs.

7.1. Background

Generalized polygons were introduced by Tits in 1959 in [43], and have seen extensive development since then, as discussed in Van Maldeghem’s book [44], Thas’ article in [42, Chapter 9], Payne and Thas’ book on generalized quadrangles [37] and elsewhere. Intuitively, the generalized nn-gon is such that every point-line pair is included in some ordinary nn-gon contained in the generalized nn-gon, and there are no ordinary mm-gons contained in the generalized nn-gon for m<nm<n. Equivalently, a generalized nn-gon has an incidence graph of diameter nn and girth 2​n2n [44].

In this paper, we are concerned with the combinatorial properties of generalized polygons much more than with their geometric structure.

Definition 7.1 (Incidence-graph representation of a point-line geometry).

Let Γ=(𝒫,ℒ,𝐈)\Gamma=(\mathcal{P},\mathcal{L},\mathbf{I}) be a point-line geometry, where 𝒫\mathcal{P} and ℒ\mathcal{L} are the sets of points and lines and 𝐈\mathbf{I} is the incidence relationship between them. An incidence-graph representation 𝔾⁡(Γ)\mathbb{G}(\Gamma) of Γ\Gamma is a graph in which V⁡(𝔾⁡(Γ))=𝒫∪ℒV(\mathbb{G}(\Gamma))=\mathcal{P}\cup\mathcal{L}, and (x,y)∈E⁡(𝔾⁡(Γ))(x,y)\in E(\mathbb{G}(\Gamma)) when x∈𝒫x\in\mathcal{P}, y∈ℒy\in\mathcal{L} and xx lies on yy, or vice versa.

Definition 7.2 (Order of a generalized nn-gon, thick nn-gon).

[44] A generalized nn-gon has order (s,t),(s,t), where every line is incident with s+1s+1 points and every point is incident to t+1t+1 lines. A generalized nn-gon is thick when both s,t>1,s,t>1, and thin otherwise.

Since a generalized polygon admitting polarity is self-dual, it has generalized-polygon order (s,t)(s,t) with s=ts=t.

Well-known results of Feit and Higman [22, Theorem 1] imply that a thick generalized nn-gon exists only when n∈{2,3,4,6,8}n\in\{2,3,4,6,8\}. Thick generalized nn-gons 𝔾n​(q,q)\mathbb{G}_{n}(q,q) admitting polarity are known to exist when n=2n=2 and q∈ℤ>1,q\in\mathbb{Z}_{>1}, n=3n=3 and qq is a prime power, n=4n=4 and q=22​m+1q=2^{2m+1} for m∈ℤ≥0m\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}, and n=6n=6 and q=32​m+1q=3^{2m+1} for m∈ℤ≥0m\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}, and cannot exist for other nn [22, Theorem 1], [44, Proposition 7.2.7].

As mentioned earlier, the incidence graphs of the Desarguesian generalized triangles 𝔾3​(q,q)\mathbb{G}_{3}(q,q) are in fact isomorphic to the bipartite compatibility graphs ℂ⁡(1,q).\mathbb{C}(1,q). Such an isomorphism cannot hold for nn-gons with nn even: these have even diameter, whereas each ℂ⁡(k,q)\mathbb{C}(k,q) has odd diameter.

7.2. Thin Polygons

Thin generalized nn-gons admitting polarity are self-dual, so must have generalized-polygon order (1,1)(1,1). These are then just ordinary nn-gons, and the incidence graph of the thin generalized nn-gon 𝔾n​(1,1)\mathbb{G}_{n}(1,1) is C2​n,C_{2n}, the cycle on 2​n2n vertices.

Proposition 7.3 classifies the polarities on 𝔾n​(1,1)\mathbb{G}_{n}(1,1), and follows immediately from [1, Section 4], since the incidence graph of the unique thin nn-gon is C2​nC_{2n}.

Proposition 7.3.

Let 𝔾=𝔾n​(1,1)\mathbb{G}=\mathbb{G}_{n}(1,1) be the unique thin generalized nn-gon admitting polarity with n∈ℤ>1n\in\mathbb{Z}_{>1}.

𝔾\mathbb{G} admits nn reflection polarities. The polarity quotient graph with respect to each reflection polarity is PnP_{n}, the path graph on nn vertices with a self-loop at each endpoint, of diameter n−1.n-1.

𝔾\mathbb{G} admits one additional rotation polarity if and only if nn is odd, rotating the vertices by π\pi radians. The polarity quotient graph with respect to the rotation polarity is CnC_{n}, the cycle graph on nn vertices with no self-loops, of diameter n−12.\frac{n-1}{2}.

There are no further polarities on 𝔾\mathbb{G}.

Proposition 7.3 shows that the diameter condition of Corollary 1.5 fails for the rotation polarity. On the other hand, it succeeds for any reflection polarity. We use Corollary 1.5, applied to thin polygons, to construct some of the large graphs in subsequent sections. We therefore use only the reflection polarity for thin generalized polygons in this paper.

To illustrate the concepts in Sections 7.1 and 7.2, the thin generalized polygon 𝔾4​(1,1)\mathbb{G}_{4}(1,1) is shown in Figure 3, with its incidence graph and polarity quotient with respect to one of the reflection polarities.

7.3. Prior Results on Generalized Polygons

The following four propositions are well-known for thick generalized polygons [44]. After applying Proposition 7.3, these propositions hold for the thin generalized polygons with respect to the reflection polarity as well. We state them here in this slightly more general context as thin polygons have been useful in the construction of a new largest graph in Section 7.8.1.

Proposition 7.4.

[44, Lemma 1.5.4] Let 𝔾=𝔾n​(q,q)\mathbb{G}=\mathbb{G}_{n}(q,q) be a generalized nn-gon. Then

  1. (1)

    Δ⁡(𝔾)=q+1,\Delta(\mathbb{G})=q+1, and

  2. (2)

    D⁡(𝔾)=n.D(\mathbb{G})=n.

Proposition 7.5.

[44, Lemma 1.5.4] Let 𝔾=𝔾n​(q,q)\mathbb{G}=\mathbb{G}_{n}(q,q) be a generalized nn-gon admitting polarity, with P⁡(𝔾)P(\mathbb{G}) its polarity quotient graph. Then |V⁡(P⁡(𝔾))|=|V⁡(P⁡(𝔾)¯)|=∑i=0n−1qi.|V(P(\mathbb{G}))|=|V(\overline{P(\mathbb{G})})|=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}q^{i}.

Proposition 7.6(1) is presented in [44, Proposition 7.2.8] and Proposition 7.6(2) in [44, Propositions 7.2.3 and 7.2.5]. Proposition 7.6(3) and (4) are discussed in [1, Section 4].

Proposition 7.6.

Let 𝔾=𝔾n​(q,q)\mathbb{G}=\mathbb{G}_{n}(q,q) be a generalized nn-gon admitting a polarity ρ\rho, and let P⁡(𝔾)P(\mathbb{G}) be its polarity quotient graph. Let NρN_{\rho} be the number of absolute vertices in the polarity quotient graph with respect to ρ\rho. Then NρN_{\rho} satisfies:

  1. (1)

    q+1≤Nρ≤q​q+1,q+1\leq N_{\rho}\leq q\sqrt{q}+1, when 𝔾\mathbb{G} is thick and n=3,n=3,

  2. (2)

    Nρ=qn2+1N_{\rho}=q^{\frac{n}{2}}+1 when 𝔾\mathbb{G} is thick and n∈{2,4,6},n\in\{2,4,6\},

  3. (3)

    Nρ=2N_{\rho}=2 when 𝔾\mathbb{G} is thin and ρ\rho is a reflection polarity, and

  4. (4)

    Nρ=0N_{\rho}=0 when 𝔾\mathbb{G} is thin, nn is odd and ρ\rho is the rotation polarity.

This accounts for every polarity on any generalized nn-gon admitting polarity.

Proposition 7.7 then follows from Propositions 7.5 and 7.6.

Proposition 7.7.

Let 𝔾=𝔾n​(q,q)\mathbb{G}=\mathbb{G}_{n}(q,q) be a generalized nn-gon admitting a polarity ρ\rho. Then 𝔾\mathbb{G} has non-absolute points with respect to ρ\rho if and only if n>2n>2.

Proposition 7.8 gives the exact diameter of the polarity quotient of a generalized nn-gon admitting polarity. This observation appears in several early papers, but to our knowledge, Loz and Pineda-Villavicencio were the first to provide a proof for thick nn-gons [35, Theorem 2.7]. Using Proposition 7.3, we extend this result to thin polygons with reflection polarity.

Proposition 7.8.

Let 𝔾\mathbb{G} be a generalized nn-gon admitting polarity. Let P⁡(𝔾)P(\mathbb{G}) be the polarity quotient graph with respect to a non-rotation polarity of 𝔾\mathbb{G}. Then D⁡(P⁡(𝔾))=D⁡(𝔾)−1D(P(\mathbb{G}))=D(\mathbb{G})-1.

We use Proposition 7.8 and Lemma 4.11 to establish the results in this paper and to construct new largest-known graphs. We develop the generalized quadrangle example in Section 7.8.1, illustrating the case where we have found a new largest-known graph of diameter 33 and degree 1818.

7.4. New Results on Generalized Polygons

We apply the general theorems of Section 5 to generalized polygons having the same diameter and derive asymptotic values for the number of vertices in graphs in these families. The advantage of using these polygons in this manner is in the fact that their polarity quotients asymptotically approach the Moore bound themselves, as shown in  [19]. Since they satisfy the theorems and corollaries in Section 5, the Kronecker products of their polarity quotients will also approach the Moore bound asymptotically, as both field orders qq and rr tend to infinity.

Corollary 7.9.

Let 𝔾m=𝔾m​(q,q)\mathbb{G}_{m}=\mathbb{G}_{m}(q,q) be a generalized mm-gon and 𝔾n=𝔾n​(r,r)\mathbb{G}_{n}=\mathbb{G}_{n}(r,r) be a generalized nn-gon, both admitting polarities, and let Pm​(𝔾m)P_{m}(\mathbb{G}_{m}) and Pn​(𝔾n)P_{n}(\mathbb{G}_{n}) be their polarity quotient graphs with respect to non-rotation polarities. Then the diameter of P⁡(𝔾m⊙𝔾n)P(\mathbb{G}_{m}\odot\mathbb{G}_{n}), the resulting composed-polarity quotient graph on 𝔾m⊙𝔾n,\mathbb{G}_{m}\odot\mathbb{G}_{n}, is D=max⁡(m,n)−1.D=\max(m,n)-1.

Proof.

By Proposition 7.4 (22), 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m} has diameter mm and 𝔾n\mathbb{G}_{n} has diameter nn, and by Proposition 7.8, D⁡(Pm​(𝔾m))=m−1D(P_{m}(\mathbb{G}_{m}))=m-1 and D⁡(Pn​(𝔾n))=n−1.D(P_{n}(\mathbb{G}_{n}))=n-1. The diameter follows from Corollary 1.5. ∎

Lemma 7.10.

Let 𝔾m​(q,q),𝔾n​(r,r),Pm​(𝔾m)⊗Pn​(𝔾n)\mathbb{G}_{m}(q,q),\mathbb{G}_{n}(r,r),P_{m}(\mathbb{G}_{m})\otimes P_{n}(\mathbb{G}_{n}) and P⁡(𝔾m⊙𝔾n)P(\mathbb{G}_{m}\odot\mathbb{G}_{n}) be as in Corollary 7.9, where at least one of m,n≠2,m,n\neq 2, and let G=P⁡(𝔾m⊙𝔾n)G=P(\mathbb{G}_{m}\odot\mathbb{G}_{n}). Then

  1. (1)

    |V⁡(G¯)|=(∑i=0m−1qi)​(∑i=0n−1ri),|V(\overline{G})|=(\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}{q^{i}})(\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}{r^{i}}), and

  2. (2)

    Δ⁡(G¯)=(q+1)​(r+1)\Delta(\overline{G})=(q+1)(r+1).

Proof.

Theorem 1.3 implies that P⁡(𝔾m⊙𝔾n)≅Pm​(𝔾m)⊗Pn​(𝔾n).P(\mathbb{G}_{m}\odot\mathbb{G}_{n})\cong P_{m}(\mathbb{G}_{m})\otimes P_{n}(\mathbb{G}_{n}). Clearly, graphs obtained by dropping all self-loops from isomorphic graphs are themselves isomorphic.
1) We use the Pm​(𝔾m​(q,q))⊗Pn​(𝔾n​(r,r))P_{m}(\mathbb{G}_{m}(q,q))\otimes P_{n}(\mathbb{G}_{n}(r,r)) construction to get the number of vertices. Removing the self-loops at this point has no effect on the number of vertices, so by Proposition 7.5 and Proposition 4.2, the number of vertices is

|V⁡(G¯)|=|V⁡(G)|=(∑i=0m−1qi)​(∑i=0n−1ri).|V(\overline{G})|=|V(G)|=\left(\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}{q^{i}}\right)\left(\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}{r^{i}}\right).

2) We use the P⁡(𝔾m​(q,q)⊙𝔾n​(r,r))P(\mathbb{G}_{m}(q,q)\odot\mathbb{G}_{n}(r,r)) construction to get the degree. Both 𝔾m​(q,q)\mathbb{G}_{m}(q,q) and 𝔾n​(r,r)\mathbb{G}_{n}(r,r) have a bipartition-reversing automorphism, so by Proposition 4.15(1) and Proposition 7.4(1), Δ⁡(𝔾m​(q,q)⊙𝔾n​(r,r))=(q+1)​(r+1).\Delta(\mathbb{G}_{m}(q,q)\odot\mathbb{G}_{n}(r,r))=(q+1)(r+1). 𝔾m​(q,q)⊙𝔾n​(r,r)\mathbb{G}_{m}(q,q)\odot\mathbb{G}_{n}(r,r) is bipartite. Since 𝔾m​(q,q)⊙𝔾n​(r,r)\mathbb{G}_{m}(q,q)\odot\mathbb{G}_{n}(r,r) is regular, all its vertices are of maximal degree (q+1)​(r+1).(q+1)(r+1). Since at least one of m,n≠2m,n\neq 2, by Proposition 7.7, there is a non-absolute vertex vv in one of the factors, so for any ww in the other factor, (v,w)(v,w) is non-absolute with respect to the composed polarity. So by Lemma 4.11,

Δ⁡(G¯)=(q+1)​(r+1).\Delta(\overline{G})=(q+1)(r+1).

∎

7.5. New Infinite Families of Large Diameter-2, -3 and -5 Graphs and Their Approach to the Moore Bound

We discuss in this section constructions from generalized nn-gons with n>2n>2. Fixing nn, we note that their degrees (q+1)→∞(q+1)\rightarrow\infty as q→∞q\rightarrow\infty, so Theorem 1.6 applies, and the graphs in the families 𝒢n\mathcal{G}_{n} approach the Moore bound as q,r→∞.q,r\rightarrow\infty.

Corollary 7.11.

Let 𝔾n​(q,q)\mathbb{G}_{n}(q,q) and 𝔾n​(r,r)\mathbb{G}_{n}(r,r) be incidence graphs of generalized nn-gons, where n∈{3,4,6}n\in\{3,4,6\}, qq and rr are such that 𝔾n​(q,q)\mathbb{G}_{n}(q,q) and 𝔾n​(r,r)\mathbb{G}_{n}(r,r) admit non-rotation polarities ρq\rho_{q} and ρr\rho_{r}. Let 𝒢n\mathcal{G}_{n} be the family of all composed-polarity quotient graphs P⁡(𝔾n​(q,q)⊙𝔾n​(r,r))¯.\overline{P(\mathbb{G}_{n}(q,q)\odot\mathbb{G}_{n}(r,r))}. Then 𝒢n\mathcal{G}_{n} is an infinite family of graphs of diameter n−1n-1 covering degrees (q+1)​(r+1)(q+1)(r+1), whose graph orders asymptotically approach the Moore bound as both qq and r→∞r\rightarrow\infty.

Proof.

The corollary follows from Proposition 7.8, Corollary 7.9 and Theorem 1.6. ∎

Theorem 1.6 is illustrated in Figure 4 for diameter-33 graphs (n=4n=4). The graph orders of the family 𝒢4,2\mathcal{G}_{4,2} approach ≈56%\approx 56\% of the Moore bound, the graph orders of the family 𝒢4,8\mathcal{G}_{4,8} approach ≈80%\approx 80\% of the Moore bound, etc.

It is easy to show that graphs constructed from quadrangles and hexagons using Corollary 7.11 exist for more degrees than in Delorme’s construction in [19]. The same holds for generalized triangles, but we do not discuss that case here. We restrict this discussion to the known thick families with parameters q=22​a+1q=2^{2a+1} for quadrangles and q=32​a+1q=3^{2a+1} for hexagons, together with the thin cases where q=1q=1.

    𝒢4:\mathcal{G}_{4}: Thick graphs in this family have degree (2k+1)​(2ℓ+1)=2k+ℓ+2k+2ℓ+1(2^{k}+1)(2^{\ell}+1)=2^{k+\ell}+2^{k}+2^{\ell}+1, where kk and ℓ\ell are odd. Let k+ℓ=2​mk+\ell=2m. When m>2m>2, their degrees fall entirely into the interval (22​m,22​m+1).(2^{2m},2^{2m+1}). This gives ⌈m2⌉\lceil{\frac{m}{2}}\rceil graphs in this degree interval. Including a graph constructed with the thin quadrangle as a factor (k=0k=0 and OPENℓ=2​m−1),\ell=2m-1), the construction covers ⌈m2⌉+1\lceil{\frac{m}{2}}\rceil+1 degrees in (22​m,22​m+1),(2^{2m},2^{2m+1}), and no other degrees within [22​m−1,22​m+1)[2^{2m-1},2^{2m+1}), as can be seen in Figure 4. (Note that the cases m=1,2m=1,2 are exceptions to this counting rule.) As in the 𝒢4\mathcal{G}_{4} case, the case m=1m=1 is an exception to this counting rule. This is in contrast to the discussion in [19], which produces exactly 11 graph having degree in [32​m−1,32​m+1).[3^{2m-1},3^{2m+1}).

7.6. Generalized 2-gons and the Infinite Family 𝒢2\mathcal{G}_{2}

We complete here the characterization of polarity quotients of Kronecker products of generalized nn-gons admitting polarity with a short discussion of Kronecker products of 22-gons. The incidence graph of G2​(q,q)G_{2}(q,q) is the balanced complete bipartite graph Kq+1,q+1K_{q+1,q+1} for any q∈ℤ>0,q\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}, and any bijection from one partition to the other extends to a polarity. All vertices of this graph are absolute under any polarity, so the degree of the quotient of the Reduced-Kronecker product of a pair of 22-gons is not the same as that of the Reduced-Kronecker product itself. This changes the calculations throughout, so the n=2n=2 case must be treated individually. However, it is trivial to show that the composed-polarity graphs of this family are complete, so are Moore graphs.

7.7. Replication of Vertices

Delorme provides a technique in [19] for replication of a set SS in a graph GG with pairwise shortest path distance of at least 33 with kk copies of SS, to obtain a new graph having order |G|+k​|S|,|G|+k|S|, degree Δ⁡(G)+k\Delta(G)+k and diameter D⁡(G)D(G), and notes that the set of absolute vertices of the polarity of a generalized quadrangle or hexagon form such a set SS. Polarity quotients of generalized quadrangles and generalized hexagons both meet the shortest-path condition, so the replication technique may be used on these graphs. We have obtained graphs nearly as large as the largest known using this technique for diameter-33 degree-1919 and -2020 graphs.

7.8. Results

7.8.1. A New Largest Diam-3 Graph

Let 𝔾4​(q,q)\mathbb{G}_{4}(q,q) denote the incidence graph of a generalized quadrangle of order (q,q)(q,q) admitting a polarity. Let G¯\overline{G} be the polarity quotient graph P⁡(𝔾4​(q1,q1)⊙𝔾4​(q2,q2))¯\overline{P(\mathbb{G}_{4}(q_{1},q_{1})\odot\mathbb{G}_{4}(q_{2},q_{2}))}. Using Corollary 7.9 and Lemma 7.10, for q1=1q_{1}=1 and q2=8q_{2}=8, we get a diameter-33, degree-1818 graph of order 23402340, which is the largest known of that degree and diameter as of October 2026. To our knowledge, the previous largest diameter-33, degree-1818 graph was a 2024 star-product construction of order 18301830 [31], and before that, the largest diameter-33, degree-1818 graph was of order 1620, cited in [34].

7.8.2. Other Results

We show this and other results in Figure 4 and Table 3. It can be seen in Figure 4 that in each interval [2a,2a+2)[2^{a},2^{a+2}) with aa odd, there is only one P​(𝔾4​(q,q))¯\overline{P(\mathbb{G}_{4}(q,q))} graph [19], but the number of P⁡(𝔾4​(q,q)⊙𝔾4​(r,r))¯\overline{P(\mathbb{G}_{4}(q,q)\odot\mathbb{G}_{4}(r,r))} graphs increases as aa increases. On the other hand, there are many more P⁡(𝔾⁡(s,t)⊙O​p​p​(𝔾⁡(s,t)))¯\overline{P(\mathbb{G}(s,t)\odot Opp(\mathbb{G}(s,t)))} graphs [20] in each interval. This is due to the plethora of generalized quadrangles 𝔾4​(s,t)\mathbb{G}_{4}(s,t) that may be used as the base bipartite graph. In contrast, we use only generalized quadrangles with qq and rr either 11 or odd powers of 22 in the P​(𝔾4​(q,q))¯\overline{P(\mathbb{G}_{4}(q,q))} and P⁡(𝔾4​(q,q)⊙𝔾4​(r,r))¯\overline{P(\mathbb{G}_{4}(q,q)\odot\mathbb{G}_{4}(r,r))} constructions, since these are the quadrangles with polarity that are known to exist.

8. Conclusions

We have shown a structural compatibility between the Kronecker product and the polarity quotient on bipartite graphs admitting polarity, and using this, have found new families of graphs, two of which exist for any even diameter 2​k2k using bipartite compatibility graphs. We have also demonstrated families of diameter 2, 3, and 5 using generalized polygons. Our degree 18, diameter 3 graph has the largest order as of October 2026.

The Moore bound is close to the best known bound for the degree-diameter problem, with better bounds differing by only 11 or 22, with a few special cases having slightly higher defects [36]. However, there are few known families of graphs that asymptotically approach the Moore bound. It is interesting to note that to our knowledge, all of the known families of graphs that asymptotically approach or meet the Moore bound have geometric constructions or interpretations, e.g., variants on the generalized polygons [4, 5, 12, 19, 20, 21, 39], and the new graphs derived from spherical buildings [14].

There are immediate applications of this theoretical work. One area of interest is that of high-performance computer networks, where large low-diameter topologies have been proposed to meet the performance and scaling requirements for modern datacenters and supercomputers [7, 30, 31, 33]. Such a network may be modeled as an undirected graph, with graph vertices as computational nodes, and graph edges as links between these nodes. Low diameter is desirable as it bounds worst-case hop count, and a large number of nodes gives higher compute performance to the system. Successful approaches to the degree-diameter problem speak directly to the design of optimal high-performance computing networks.

The polarity discussion in Section 6 was directed by the authors, who noted that bipartite compatibility graphs do have polarities having the needed properties, and was guided by an inquiry into the nature of these polarities. Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
